one_line_contribution: That the memory-injection budget k is not only an accuracy lever but a *variance* lever, so a prompt optimizer searching over a k=7 agent captures a strictly larger fraction of its reported validation gain as pure selection bias than at k=0 — measured with a null (identity/paraphrase-proposal) optimizer paired by optimizer seed — plus a measured decomposition of whether common random numbers survive interactive rollouts at all.
closest_prior_work: Three bodies threaten different pieces, and the proposal has already conceded two of them. (1) Dodge et al., 'Show Your Work' (2019) and its follow-up 'Expected Validation Performance and Estimation of a Random Variable's Maximum' (NAACL 2021) own the max-of-N inflation mechanism and the budget-indexed reporting rule; the proposal disclaims this outright, which is honest but removes the mechanism from the contribution. (2) The track's own prior null replicate and 5-14 point re-scoring spread own the phenomenon; P6 is self-labelled replication. (3) The threat to what *remains* is the long-context/distraction literature — Liu et al., 'Lost in the Middle' (2023), Shi et al., 'Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context' (2023), Levy et al., 'Same Task, More Tokens' (2024) — which already establishes that more injected context degrades and destabilizes generation. P1 ('k=7 lengthens trajectories and inflates sigma') is close to a restatement of that in agent clothing, and the proposal offers no arm that separates 'memory items' from 'more tokens.' A fourth threat is to the *instrument*: Sclar et al. (ICLR 2024) and Mizrahi et al. (TACL 2024) show semantics-preserving prompt variation produces large, real accuracy swings, which undercuts the assumption that a judge-verified-paraphrase null arm measures only selection bias.
strongest_objection: Both primary novelty claims are underpowered by construction, and the proposal says so itself. P1 estimates a variance ratio from 8 replicates per cell: with ~7 df on each side, the 95% CI for a variance ratio spans roughly a factor of 5, so sigma(k=7)/sigma(k=0) must be observed at ~2.2x before the CI on the ratio excludes 1 — yet P1 predicts 1.3x. Measurement note 7 concedes 'a true ratio near 1.3 may go undetected,' meaning a *primary* prediction is designed so that its own predicted effect size is undetectable, at a cost of 9,600 rollouts. P2 is worse: it is a 4-pair paired test, and the claimed MDE of ~2.8 points appears to have been imported from the n=1,200 item-level McNemar calculation in note 1. A one-sample t-test with n=4 needs d~2.2, so at the stated between-run SD of 1.5 the true MDE is ~3.4 points and higher still if the paired-difference SD (not the between-run SD) is 1.5*sqrt(2); the pre-registered threshold of 3 points sits below it. Compounding this, the headline is confounded: score variance for a binary metric is p(1-p)/m, so if k=7 moves accuracy toward 0.5 (the track's prior work says injection at 7 items *harms* accuracy), sigma rises mechanically and the 'coupling' is a base-rate artifact, not evidence that memory volume amplifies the curse. Reporting bias in accuracy points rather than in sigma units makes this indistinguishable. The result is a plan whose well-powered components (E2's cached tensor, E3's design rule) are self-labelled replication, baseline transport, or derived from the underpowered E0/E1 inputs, while the parts carrying the novelty claim will most likely return 'not detected.'
what_would_fix_it: Reallocate the envelope toward the claim that carries the novelty. (1) Add a content-matched placebo at k=7 (shuffled/off-query retrieved items, or token-matched filler) so P1 can attribute variance inflation to retrieved experience rather than to context length — without it P1 is a known long-context result. (2) Fix P1's estimator: 8 replicates cannot resolve 1.3x. Either raise replicates to ~30 per cell (these are cheap eval rollouts; the 48,000-rollout E2 tensor is oversized relative to K=20 candidates) or estimate sigma from the m-subsampling curve with a paired bootstrap across k on shared items. (3) Make P2 an actual interaction: run E1 at k in {0,3,7}, since the track's own causal lever is the 3-vs-7 contrast, and buy optimizer seeds by cutting generations (8x12x50 = 4,800 rollouts per run; halving generations roughly doubles seeds). (4) Report null gain standardized by the condition's own sigma, and drop 'curse fraction' as the primary derived quantity — it is a ratio whose denominator (real gain) the proposal's own Risk 1 admits may be near zero, so its 4-seed interval is meaningless. (5) State and test the transport assumption that null-arm bias estimates real-arm bias: the exact-copy null has perfectly correlated candidates, the real arm does not, and the correlation discount in P7 is exactly what differs between them — move ablation (f) into E1 rather than E2. (6) Demote the EB rank-preservation 'separation' to a remark, or state it correctly: shrinkage toward a common mean is rank-preserving only under homoskedastic candidate variances, and binomial variance p(1-p)/m is not homoskedastic even at equal m, so the 'analytic' claim is either trivial or false as written. (7) Run the literature search before spending compute, as pre-registered.
missing_baseline: A content-matched / length-matched placebo injection arm at k=7: seven retrieved items that are topically plausible but query-irrelevant (or shuffled across items, or token-matched filler), evaluated in both E0 and E1. Without it, every P1/P2 effect is equally explained by 'longer, more distractable contexts' and the paper's claim to belong to the memory track collapses. Secondarily, E1 omits k=3 entirely, so the design cannot show that selection bias tracks the same dose-response curve (harm at 7, none at 3) that motivated the whole proposal — a two-point contrast cannot distinguish a monotone volume effect from an arbitrary threshold. A third gap: E2b compares ten selection rules on a pool of only K=20 candidates, all harvested from the four real k=7 runs; the bootstrap over the candidate pool, not over the 1,200 items, is the binding interval, and 20 survivorship-selected candidates cannot resolve the 1-2 point differences P4 predicts.
preprint_collision: The check is a self-declared failure: zero searches completed, zero titles retrieved, for the second consecutive round, with the authors correctly refusing to call that novelty. Per the standard that an unsearched novelty claim is a weakness rather than a neutral, this alone caps novelty. I credit the honesty and the pre-registered kill clause ('if a paper reports both the k-interaction and the CRN item/seed decomposition, the project is killed'), but a proposal cannot outsource its own novelty verification to a post-acceptance appendix. I cannot verify 2026 preprints, so I state only what I can: the exact niche the authors themselves flag as highest-risk — evaluation-noise floors for LLM agents, winner's-curse and multiple-comparison corrections for prompt optimizers, and statistical protocols for LLM evals — is demonstrably active and already has anchored entries (Miller, 'Adding Error Bars to Evals,' arXiv 2411.00640; Madaan et al., 'Quantifying Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks,' 2024; Card et al., 'With Little Power Comes Great Responsibility,' EMNLP 2020; Dodge et al., NAACL 2021), none of which appear in the Related Work despite bearing directly on the MDE, power, and shrinkage arguments the proposal builds its protocol on. Their absence suggests the background-knowledge pass was as incomplete as the search. The burden is on the authors to show the k x selection-bias interaction and the item/seed CRN decomposition are unclaimed; as submitted, that burden is unmet.
